blocks.x: The contracted seams that make automation real: typed contracts across ERP, CRM, ITSM and comms, replayable failure handling, rate-limit aware traffic shaping and monitors that catch API drift before the month-end close does.
Automation dies in the seams, not in the agents

Integration is where hyperautomation programs actually die: not in the models, but in the seam where an agent writes to an ERP that changed its API on Thursday. We treat every seam as a contract with direction, schema, identity, rate limits, failure behavior and a drift monitor — and the contract is versioned like code.

The practice covers the unglamorous essentials: replayable failure queues, idempotency keys on every write, rate-limit shaping, sandbox parity, and the monitors that notice API drift before the business users notice stuck work.
Below: the failure modes that break integrations at the worst moment, the reference architecture of contracted seams, and the console that keeps seam health visible through month-end load.
Four failure modes that break seams at month-end
Every one of these fires during peak load, which is exactly when nobody can afford it — the countermeasures are contractual and structural, not heroic.

blocks.x: Reference architecture — typed seams with replay and drift monitors

Seams are contracts, not credentials: typed request/response schemas, idempotency keys, replay queues and drift monitors that diff live API behavior against the contract — so a vendor's silent change is caught by a monitor, not by a failed close.

blocks.title: Reference architecture — contracted integration plane
blocks.note: Contract tests run in CI against sandbox on every vendor release notification — the drift monitor is the smoke detector, the contract test is the fire drill.

blocks.x: One write across three systems, guaranteed once

From the automation's action through contract validation, rate shaping and the idempotent write to the replay path when a system rejects mid-flight — including where duplicates would otherwise be born.

blocks.title: Seam lifecycle — contract, shape, key, guard, replay, monitor
blocks.note: Failures land in replay queues with their full request context; replay is a supervised action, not an auto-retry storm.

widgets.title: The integration fabric — click nodes for contract posture

nodes.label: SaaS estate
nodes.detail: Connectors via iPaaS with schema validation at the edge — a payload that fails schema never enters the backbone.

nodes.label: Core systems
nodes.detail: ERP/CRM exposure through contract-first APIs; direct DB links are denied by network policy, not by convention.

nodes.label: Event backbone
nodes.detail: Kafka with replay per topic; retention sized for reconciliation windows, not for convenience.

nodes.label: Contract registry
nodes.detail: Schema-first contracts with compatibility gates; producers cannot break consumers silently.

nodes.label: API actuation
nodes.detail: Sync paths for request-response business steps; timeouts and budgets per route.

nodes.label: RPA surface
nodes.detail: Reserved for closed surfaces; each bot registered with its UI map version and owner — a bot is a liability until proven otherwise.

nodes.label: Agent actuation
nodes.detail: Judgement-heavy steps with human-grade evidence packets; agents call the same registry as any other actuator.

nodes.label: Downstream targets
nodes.detail: Idempotent sinks with reconciliation jobs — the fabric assumes at-least-once delivery and proves exactly-once effects.

widgets.note: Click nodes to read each lane's contract posture. RPA sits in the same registry as APIs — same monitoring, same ownership, same audit story.

widgets.title: Estate consolidation what-if — point-to-point vs fabric
widgets.note: Metcalfe's law is the debt curve: fragility grows with the square of systems under point-to-point, near-linearly under a fabric. Drag the P2P share down and watch the same estate become maintainable.

blocks.note: Reference program model: fragility indices and targets from delivery diagnostics, not client telemetry.
